title: Length-aware selectivity for substring contains() scan filters
summary:
The q09 benchmark went from 1075.0 ms to 698.2 ms (-35.0%) in the bench quick check (2 parameter bindings, 4 hot runs each). Results matched the current best. Single-query profile of q09.m0: 1.93s before, 1.17s after.

The change is in RelationStatisticsHelper::InspectTableFilter (src/optimizer/join_order/relation_statistics_helper.cpp). I added a case for EXPRESSION_FILTER that estimates selectivity for contains(col, 'literal'):
- It only matches when the column is a column ref and the second argument is a non-NULL, non-empty VARCHAR constant.
- Estimate = ceil(cardinality × max(0.2 × 0.75^L, 0.01)), at least 1 row, where L is the literal length (capped at 64).
- Every other expression filter, including NOT and OR, still returns the input cardinality, so the default 0.2 fallback is unchanged for them.
- The existing CONJUNCTION_AND case already takes the minimum over its children, so contains ANDed with other filters on the same column is covered.
I added one include (expression_filter.hpp).

The plan change in q09 differs from what the issue expected:
- Before: lineitem was probed against a part-only build side, then probed the orders build side (15M rows, 3.63s) and the partsupp⋈supplier⋈nation build side (8M rows, 3.04s).
- After: part⋈partsupp (436K rows, partsupp reduced by a Bloom filter from part) is the build side for the lineitem probe (join 2.36s). The 3.27M-row result of that join is the build side for the orders join, with orders probing it (1.84s). Supplier⋈nation is joined last (0.03s).
- So the orders join flipped as hoped. The partsupp join was not flipped; the join order was rearranged so partsupp joins part first.

I only ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on q09.m0. The other three instances are covered only by the bench timing, not by a plan check.
notes: In the new q09 plan the lineitem scan no longer has a Bloom filter: it emits all 60M rows (3.28s scan) into a join that keeps 3.27M. Before, it had a Bloom filter on l_partkey from part. The next step is to push a Bloom filter from the part⋈partsupp build side (both keys, or at least the part key) onto the lineitem scan, which could save a lot more. The orders join (1.84s) is now probed by orders, which is where the issue's "BF on flipped probe" idea applies.

title: Bloom filter on first equality key of multi-condition hash joins
summary:
Hash joins with more than one equality key can now push a bloom filter on their first key into the probe-side table scan. Before this, the bloom filter only existed for single-key joins. Two .cpp files changed, no header changes.

1) In join_hashtable.cpp, JoinHashTable::InsertHashes: for multi-key joins, the bloom filter is no longer fed the combined row hash. Instead it gathers layout column 0 (condition 0's build key) from the chunk's row locations, hashes it with VectorOperations::Hash and inserts those hashes. Single-key joins are unchanged.
2) In physical_hash_join.cpp, CanUseBloomFilter now requires cmp == EQUAL and ht->conditions[0].comparison == EQUAL, replacing the conditions.size()==1 check. FinalizeFilters only offers the bloom filter for the filter whose join_condition[filter_idx] == 0. All other guards are kept: filtered build side, probe estimate larger than the build count, no cast, not a perfect hash table, in-memory only. The probe-side filter already uses conditions[0] for its key name and type and NullValuesAreEqual(0).

Measured with bench (2 bindings, 4 hot runs each): q09 went from 669.6 ms to 528.3 ms (-21.1%); a separate q09-only run gave -18.4%. The geomean over the visible templates is -21.1%.

Correctness checks, each compared against the same query written with `col+0` keys so no filter can be pushed down. All results matched:
- a 2-key INNER join of the large fact table against a filtered composite-key table;
- the same with NULLs injected into build key 1;
- a RIGHT join with NULLs injected into build key 0.

A VARCHAR-first-key check also ran, but both versions returned 0 rows, so it tells us nothing. I did not add a sqllogictest because test/ is off limits.
notes:
The filter is only ever on condition 0. When condition 0 is unselective but a later key is selective, there is no gain. A follow-up could build the filter on whichever equality key has the most selective min/max or the fewest distinct values, but then the build-side gather has to match the probe column exactly.

Testing tip: range()/CTE sources don't receive pushed-down filters, so they don't exercise the bloom filter. Use real table scans and compare against a `col+0 = col+0` version, which blocks pushdown.

Correctness depends on the build side hashing exactly layout column 0 with VectorOperations::Hash, the same function BFTableFilter uses on the probe side. Build rows with a NULL key 0 only add false positives, which is harmless.

title: Offset-aware join filter pushdown through CM integral compress projections (min/max + BF)
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q09 +4.7%; needs at least -5%)
summary:
Join filters (the min/max range and the bloom filter) can now be pushed down through compressed-materialization projections of the form `__internal_compress_integral_*(x, offset)`. Before this, that projection blocked filter pushdown completely.

Changes:
- **Optimizer** (`PushdownJoinFilterExpression`): accepts one level of the compress function when its offset is a non-NULL constant castable to BIGINT and its input is integral, at most 64 bits, and not UBIGINT. The offset is stored as a `Value offset` on `JoinFilterPushdownColumn`, and it is also copied when the column is rewritten for UNION children.
- **Hash join** (`FinalizeFilters`): min/max are cast to HUGEINT, the offset is added, and the result is cast to the storage type; if any cast fails the filter is skipped. The IN-list filter is skipped when there is an offset. The bloom filter is allowed when both the key type and the storage type are integral, at most 64 bits, and the storage type is not UBIGINT. `PushBloomFilter`, which also serves the deferred path, passes the offset of the first condition's column to the filter.
- **Bloom filter** (`BFTableFilter`): gets a `has_key_offset`/`key_offset` pair, carried through Copy and Serialize (optional fields 203/204). When it is set, each key is computed as `(uint64(int64(v)) - offset)`, masked to the key type's width, written into a scratch UBIGINT vector that keeps the NULL markers, and then hashed with `VectorOperations::Hash`. This gives the same hash as the hash table's `Hash<uintN>(compressed key)`. `FilterValue` applies the same translation. `CheckStatistics` returns NO_PRUNING_POSSIBLE when there is an offset.
- **TopN optimizer and RowGroupPruner**: these also call `GetPushdownFilterTargets`, so they now bail out if a target column has an offset.

Measured on q09.m0 (profile): the orders scan now gets `>=`/`<=` range filters and a bloom filter, and its output drops from 15M to 2.96M rows. The o_orderkey hash join drops from 2.22s to 1.88s CPU.

Bench: q09 went from 570.3 to 523.3 ms (**-8.2%**). That is well short of the -12..-25% the hypothesis predicted (see notes).

Correctness checks:
- The bench result check passed for q09.
- A count/sum query on a compressed orders–lineitem join returned the same results as the same query with `+0` keys, and its plan confirmed the offset bloom filter was active.
- A part/lineitem join gave matching results with and without `+0`.
- I could not test negative-min keys, keys starting at a large non-zero min, or NULL keys: the tool only gives a read-only database, so I could not create test tables.
notes:
The gain was smaller than predicted. Cutting the probe rows by 80% only lowered the HJ from 2.22s to 1.88s CPU. The orders scan (0.87s) plus bloom filter evaluation now costs about the same as the join, so it is the next cost to look at.

The lineitem scan (4.76s CPU) is still the dominant operator in q09.

TopN and RowGroupPruner reuse `GetPushdownFilterTargets`. Any future pass-through that transforms values must be rejected in those two callers, or their filters would compare against the wrong values.

The scratch vector for the translated keys reuses `BFTableFilterState::found_v`, which was previously unused. This avoided editing `table_filter_state.hpp`, and it is re-initialised whenever the batch is larger than the current capacity.

title: Exact key bitmap mode for join BF on dense integer build keys
summary:
I added an exact key-bitmap mode to the join Bloom filter (BF) and it is ready to judge. When the build keys are integers that fit in 64 bits (8/16/32/64-bit signed, or 8/16/32-bit unsigned) and their range is dense, the filter becomes a bitmap indexed by (key - min) instead of a hashed filter. The tree builds, and `dbe-tool bench` shows q09 at 566.5 → 512.6 ms (-9.5%) on the first run and 553.0 → 484.5 ms (-12.4%) on the full bench. The profile of q09.m0 shows the lineitem scan's CPU time falling from 5.28s to 4.55s; it now outputs exactly 3,269,453 rows because the bitmap has no false positives. The partsupp scan also gets an exact filter.

What changed:
- `bloom_filter.hpp/.cpp`: `SetKeyRange(min, range)` switches the filter to exact mode before `Initialize`, which then allocates one bit per value in [min, max]. `InsertKeys` sets bits atomically (fetch_or). `LookupKeys`/`LookupKey` test bits on the raw key values with no hashing, and keys outside the range are rejected.
  - In `BFTableFilter::Filter`, exact mode reads keys through `UnifiedVectorFormat`. If a selection is set and the vector is not flat (for example a SEQUENCE vector), it slices first, as the hash path does.
  - `FilterValue` and `CheckStatistics` have exact-mode versions. `CheckStatistics` prunes when the zone-map range does not overlap the bitmap range, and otherwise probes up to 2048 values as before. It never returns always-false if NULLs must pass (`IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`) and the segment can contain NULLs.
- `join_hashtable.cpp` (`InsertHashes`): in exact mode it gathers layout column 0 (the first key), skips NULLs and sets the bits.
- `physical_hash_join.cpp` (`FinalizeFilters`): when the BF is deferred, `TrySetExactBloomFilterRange` uses the build-side min/max. Exact mode is used only if build and probe have the same physical type, the min/max types match the build key type, the type is one of those above, the range is under 2^31 and at most 128 bits per key in the hash table. Otherwise the existing hashed BF is used unchanged.

Correctness checks I ran: temp-table joins with NULLs and negative keys, using `=`, `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` and an `IN` subquery, matched the same joins on `+0` expressions (which don't push a filter into the scan). However, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on that temp-table query showed no BF filter on the probe scan, so the exact path's NULL and negative-key handling was not exercised. The exact path is only confirmed working by the q09 profile and the matching bench results.
notes:
- **Gain:** a sibling run found the 128 bits/key cap mattered for q21. Here the q09 build is about 436K rows over a range of about 2M, roughly 4.6 bits/key, well under the cap. The exact filter also removes the BF's false positives, so slightly fewer rows reach the lineitem→part/partsupp join (0.95s).
- **Remaining cost:** the lineitem scan is still 4.55s CPU, mostly decoding the six projected columns. The o_orderkey=l_orderkey join is 2.46s and is the next largest operator.
- **Defensive throw:** an out-of-range insert in exact mode throws an InternalException rather than silently dropping the key. That can only happen if the build-side min/max misses some hash-table rows, which the current sink path does not allow.
- **Review nit:** `TemplatedCheckStatisticsExact` has an unneeded extra brace block; it is harmless.

title: Exact-bitmap join filter through CM integral compress projections (offset-shifted, no hashed BF)
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q09 -7.9%; needs at least -5%)
summary:
The orders scan in q09 now gets an exact-bitmap join filter through the compressed-materialization projection. The release build succeeds. `bench q09`: 525.1 ms → 449.9 ms (-14.3%), with results checked by the harness. In the profile the orders scan shows `o_orderkey IN BF(l_orderkey)` plus shifted min/max filters, and its output falls from 15M to 2.94M rows.

Changes:
1. **Optimizer** (`PushdownJoinFilterExpression`): it now accepts `__internal_compress_integral_*(x, const)` when x is an integral type of 64 bits or less and not UBIGINT, and the constant is non-NULL and castable to BIGINT. Only one offset is allowed per column. The offset is recorded as a new `Value offset` field on `JoinFilterPushdownColumn` and copied when UNION children are rewritten. TopN and RowGroupPruner bail out on targets that have an offset.
2. **FinalizeFilters**: for offset columns, min/max are cast to HUGEINT, shifted by the offset, then cast to the storage type; the column is skipped if a cast fails. The IN filter is skipped. The bloom filter is pushed only if `TrySetExactBloomFilterRange` (called with the compressed build min/max) makes the hash table's filter exact and the storage type is one the exact lookup supports. A hashed bloom filter is never pushed for an offset column.
3. **BFTableFilter**: new `has_key_offset`/`key_offset`, serialized as optional fields 203 and 204. `Filter`, `FilterValue` and `CheckStatistics` test bit `(v - offset - key_min)` in wrapping uint64 arithmetic. The stats range check uses hugeint. If the filter is somehow not exact, an offset filter lets every row through in release builds (`D_ASSERT` in debug).
4. **PushBloomFilter**: passes the first key's offset and storage type.

Correctness checks (orders⋈lineitem with lineitem-side filters, grouped by year, compared with `o_orderkey+0=l_orderkey+0` versions): count, sum(o_totalprice) and sum(o_orderkey) match exactly in two cases.
- Sparse build: 171k rows over a 60M key range. No bitmap is built; only the shifted min/max filter is used.
- Dense build: 1.54M rows. The exact bitmap is used and orders drops from 15M to 1.47M rows.

The only offset tested was 1, because every integer key in this dataset has min 1 or 0. A wrong sign would shift by 2 and break the match above.
notes:
- **Remaining cost is the build:** the orders HASH_JOIN still shows about 1.35s CPU in the profile even though probe rows fell from 15M to 2.94M. The wall-clock gain comes mainly from the cheaper probe pipeline (scan plus projection), not from the join operator itself. A next step would target the 3.27M-row build: inserts or pointer-table size, or a perfect hash join on the compressed uint32 key, whose range is about 60M.
- **Earlier attempt (E0003):** the same pushdown with a hashed bloom filter was +4.7% on bench; the exact bitmap is what makes it pay off.
- **Fewer changes than the plan expected:** the exact-range check needed no relaxing, because passing the condition's (compressed) type as the probe type already matches the build layout type. The actual probe vector physical type is handled in `LookupKeys`.
- **Possible follow-ups:** joins with larger key offsets were not exercised here and could be worth a test with synthetic data. Pushing offsets through decompress→compress chains is another possible extension.

title: Re-land exact-bitmap join filter through CM compress (E0005) plus group prefetch in the HT probe and build
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q09 -5.7%; needs at least -5%)
summary:
I re-landed Part A (the join filter through compressed-materialization integral compression) and dropped Part B (prefetch) because it had no measurable effect.

Measured q09 bench against the current best across three runs: -11.8% (502→443 ms), -15.6% (525→444, that build had prefetch compiled in but switched off), and the final tree -9.2% (508→461). In the q09 profile, the orders scan now gets a shifted min/max filter plus an exact-bitmap BF and drops from 15.0M to 2.92M rows. The orders hash join goes from 1.59s to 1.28s CPU.

What changed:
(1) The join filter optimizer now follows the probe key through `__internal_compress_integral_*(x, const)`. It requires x to be an integral of at most 64 bits, not UBIGINT, and the constant to be non-NULL and castable to BIGINT. It records a `Value offset` on JoinFilterPushdownColumn, copies it into UNION child rewrites, and allows only one offset per column. TopN and RowGroupPruner bail out when a target has an offset.
(2) In FinalizeFilters, for offset columns, min/max are cast to HUGEINT, the offset is added, and the result is cast to the storage type; the column is skipped if a cast fails. The IN filter is skipped. A BF is pushed only after TrySetExactBloomFilterRange makes the HT filter exact and the storage type is INT8..INT64 or UINT8..UINT32. A hashed BF is never pushed for an offset column.
(3) BFTableFilter gets has_key_offset/key_offset, serialized as optional fields 203/204. Filter, FilterValue and CheckStatistics test the bit for (v - offset) in wrapping uint64 arithmetic, and the statistics range check uses hugeint. A non-exact filter with an offset lets every row through.
(4) PushBloomFilter passes the offset and the storage key type.

Part B, prefetch in join_hashtable.cpp (HT entries during probe and build, row pointers before RowMatcher, gated on a pointer table of at least 1MB), was implemented and measured: +0.1% on its own, and 443.0 vs 443.5 ms with and without it on top of Part A. I removed it entirely.

Correctness: the bench result check passes. Two q09-shaped variants with different offsets (o_orderkey > 1234567, and BETWEEN 30M AND 45M with other p_name patterns) give results identical to `+0` (no-compression) versions of the same queries, checked with EXCEPT ALL in both directions; the second check ran on the final tree. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the offset of 1234567 being applied to the min/max filter: the dynamic filter reads l_orderkey>=1234592.
notes:
- At session start, `dbe-tool profile` showed the previous session's E0005 binary: the orders scan already had a BF and 2.94M rows. After `dbe-tool build` the real current best showed 15M rows. Rebuild before trusting a baseline profile.
- Software prefetch (group pre-pass) in the join HT probe and build gave 0% on q09, with a 3.27M-row build and an ~8M-entry pointer table. The orders HJ cost is not bound by cache misses that software prefetch can fix; out-of-order execution already overlaps the independent per-row misses. Don't retry it.
- The offset arithmetic can only cause false positives, never false negatives: matching rows have exact in-range bit indices, and wrap-around only makes extra rows pass.
- Next targets in q09: the lineitem scan (~2.5-3.6s CPU), the 1.28s orders HJ (mostly build-side inserts of 3.27M rows), and the l_partkey/l_suppkey HJ (0.5s).
